title: Probing Residual Noise at a Decoherence Sweet Spot in a $^{28}$Si/SiGe Spin Qubit
authors: Shinwoo Lee, Hanseo Sohn, Jaemin Park, Hyeongyu Jang, Jonginn Yun, Jun Yoneda, Lucas E. A. Stehouwer, Davide Degli Esposti, Giordano Scappucci, Dohun Kim
abstract: In $^{28}$Si/SiGe spin qubits with micromagnets, the longitudinal stray field gradient transduces charge noise into qubit frequency noise and limits coherence. We compare two neighboring qubits in the same device with 800 ppm residual $^{29}$Si, one near a decoherence sweet spot where the gradient is locally minimized and the other at a position with a larger gradient. At the sweet spot, $T_2^*$ reaches 67 $μ\mathrm{s}$ and the Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill coherence time reaches 4.6 ms, whereas $T_2^*$ is 5.2 $μ\mathrm{s}$ at the neighboring qubit. Near 1 Hz, the frequency noise power spectral density at the sweet spot is nearly two orders of magnitude lower than at the neighboring qubit. The magnitude and low-frequency decay of the residual spectrum are compatible with the prediction for $^{29}$Si nuclear spin noise, and the weak interqubit correlation indicates that local noise becomes important for dephasing at the sweet spot. Despite a finite correlation with the charge sensor, sweet-spot operation strongly reduced the transduction of charge noise, bringing the residual frequency noise close to the level predicted for $^{29}$Si nuclear spin fluctuations.
summary: This experiment investigates noise limitations in Si/SiGe spin qubits by comparing coherence at a specially engineered 'decoherence sweet spot' versus a neighboring site. By minimizing the coupling between charge noise and qubit frequency, the researchers achieved significantly longer coherence times. The residual noise spectrum at the sweet spot strongly matches theoretical predictions for $^{29}	ext{Si}$ nuclear spin noise, confirming the effectiveness of sweet-spot operation.
main_problem: The study aims to characterize and mitigate residual noise sources that limit the coherence time of electron spin qubits in Si/SiGe heterostructures.
main_result: Operating the qubit at a 'decoherence sweet spot' significantly suppresses the coupling between charge noise and qubit frequency noise, bringing residual noise levels close to the fundamental limit set by $^{29}	ext{Si}$ nuclear spin fluctuations.
method: Coherence times ($T_2^*$, $T_2^{	ext{CPMG}}$) and noise power spectral densities (PSDs) are measured by comparing qubits at different locations relative to the local electric field gradient.
model_or_system: The system uses electron spin qubits in $^{28}	ext{Si/SiGe}$ quantum dots, where coherence is limited by the transduction of charge noise via the local stray field gradient. The analysis compares measurements at a sweet spot (low gradient) versus a neighboring site (high gradient).
key_observables: Coherence times ($T_2^*$, $T_2^{	ext{CPMG}}$), Frequency Noise Power Spectral Density $S(f)$, and Qubit-sensor cross-correlation strength $r_i(f)$.
important_parameters: Residual $^{29}	ext{Si}$ concentration ($\approx 800$ ppm), Sweet Spot condition (minimal field gradient), and frequency noise spectral shape ($1/f^2$ decay).
main_assumptions: The noise analysis often relies on approximations for noise extraction from CPMG sequences and the assumption of mutual uncorrelation between different noise sources for cross-correlation analysis.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison of coherence times and noise spectra between qubits at different gradient regimes, showing the dramatic improvement at the sweet spot and matching the predicted nuclear spin noise spectrum.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares coherence measurements (Ramsey/CPMG) between two neighboring qubits, quantifies the reduction in noise susceptibility at the sweet spot, and finally performs detailed noise spectroscopy to identify the residual noise source as $^{29}	ext{Si}$ nuclear spin fluctuations.
why_interesting: This work provides crucial experimental validation of noise mitigation techniques in solid-state qubits, demonstrating how engineering the physical environment (finding a sweet spot) can suppress environmental coupling mechanisms, which is vital for scaling quantum processors.
